cells.Definition / Overview: Self-limited irritation & swelling of upper airways
cells.Etiology: Rhinovirus (most common), others: influenza, adenovirus, enterovirus, RSV; 15% bacterial (GAS pharyngitis)
cells.Risk Factors / Epidemiology: Close child contact, asthma, allergic rhinitis, smoking, immunocompromised, anatomical anomalies
cells.Pathophysiology: Droplet inhalation → onset 10–12h → last 7-10 d up to 3 weeks →inflammation → vasodilation & ↑ permeability → nasal congestion/rhinorrhea
cells.Clinical Presentation: Cough, runny nose, sneezing, sore throat, nasal congestion, headache, malaise, myalgias, no/low fever, facial pressure
cells.Diagnostics: Clinical dx; no routine tests; rapid strep if suspected
cells.Treatment / Management: Symptom relief: decongestants, antihistamines (1st gen for sneezing), antitussives (limited), bronchodilator if wheezing, antipyretics if fever; No antibiotics
cells.Patient Education / Prevention: Hand hygiene, cough etiquette, avoid sharing, balanced diet, immunizations, balanced diet
cells.Complications:
Rare; usually self-limited

Antibiotic caution: 
-Fluoroquinolones = tendon rupture, QT prolong, photosen
-macrolides= QT prolong
-tetracyclines & sulfonamides=  photosensitivity

cells.Definition / Overview: IgE-mediated nasal inflammation; seasonal or perennial
cells.Etiology: Pollens, fungi, dust mites, dander, occupational allergens
cells.Pathophysiology: IgE response to allergen → histamine release
cells.Clinical Presentation:
Sneezing, watery rhinorrhea, congestion, itchy/watery eyes, fatigue
Salute, shiners, dennie-morgan lines, boggy/pal turbinates
cells.Diagnostics: Clinical diagnosis ; allergy skin test (preferred), IgE levels
cells.Treatment / Management:
Allergy Avoidance!!
First-line: intranasal steroids (nasonex, fluticasone) ; oral antihistamines, decongestants; referral if persistent despite treatment
cells.Patient Education / Prevention: Allergy diary, allergen avoidance, safe med use, proper nasal spray technique, hydration and  handwashing

cells.Definition / Overview: Non-immune nasal inflammation;
cells.Etiology: Irritants (cold air, odors, weather, stress, foods, meds)
cells.Clinical Presentation: Perennial nasal congestion, watery discharge; no itching; PE: erythematous nasal mucosa - how it is differentiated from allergic rhinitis
cells.Treatment / Management: Avoid triggers; decongestants; saline irrigation; intranasal steroids
cells.Patient Education / Prevention: Avoid chronic decongestant use; avoid triggers

cells.Definition / Overview:
Inflammation of paranasal sinuses + 
nasal mucosa

Viral = s/sx < 4 weeks, rhino, flu, paraflu

Bacterial = s/sx 4-12 weeks, secondary bacterial infection AFTER viral illness (S. pneumonia) 

Allergic = rhinitis symptoms WITH sore throat and cough 

Fungal= rapidly progressive, affects immunocomp + uncontrolled diabetes -> URGENT ENT referral
cells.Etiology: Viral (most common), bacterial (S. pneumo, H. flu, M. catarrhalis), fungal in immunocompromised
cells.Risk Factors / Epidemiology:
~30M/yr in US; women > men; 45–64y; smoking, allergies, dental disease, air travel, immunodef, dental disease.

Rhinovirus & parainfluenza -> fall late spring
RSV, coronavirus -> winter,spring 
Enteroviruses -> summer/ year round 
Adenoviruses -> outbreaks
cells.Pathophysiology: Viral/bacterial infection → nose blowing pushes infected secretions into sinuses → impaired drainage/ciliary function causes nasal obstruction and prolonged
cells.Clinical Presentation:
Congestion, purulent rhinorrhea, postnasal drip, facial pain/pressure, dental pain, halitosis, fever, hyposmia, fatigue, hyposomia/anosmia

Frontal = pain/tenderness lower forehead 
Maxillary = pain over cheeks, teeth, worse leaning forward
Ethmoid= pain over bridge of nose, behind eye 
Sphenoid = retro-orbital pain
cells.Diagnostics: Clinical; CT(no contrast)  if complicated; MRI for soft tissue/intracranial complications; no routine labs
cells.Patient Education / Prevention:
Correct nasal steroid use, avoid sniffing, hand hygiene, smoking cessation, no antibiotics for viral, followup in 2-3 days 
Warn SE for 1st gen antihistamines, NSAIDs, decongestants/ cough suppressants 

Enviro control, increased humidified air and fluid intake, warm compress for pressure relief, avoid swimming/ diving, smoking cessation, freq handwashing
cells.Complications: Bacterial Specific: Osteomyelitis, orbital infection, visual loss, intracranial abscess, meningitis

cells.Definition / Overview: Inflamed eyelid bump (internal or external)
cells.Clinical Presentation: Painful, red, swollen eyelid; tearing, gritty sensation, photophobia
cells.Diagnostics: Clinical = eyelid red/swollen, conjunctiva injected, cornea/pupil normal, vision normal
cells.Treatment: Warm compresses ( 5min several times/day), hygiene; avoid squeezing
cells.Patient Education: No makeup/contacts; good hygiene; no squeezing

cells.Clinical Presentation: Little to no redness; Painless, rubbery eyelid nodule; non-tender,
cells.Diagnostics: Clinical = lesion on conjunctival side, cornea/pupil/vision normal
cells.Treatment: Warm compresses; refer if >4 wks or recurrent
cells.Patient Education: Avoid touching eye; hygiene

cells.Definition / Overview: Inflammation of eyelid margins leaving scales on eye lashes
cells.Clinical Presentation: Itchy/burning lids, crusting, “pink eye”, redness, tearing, photophobia, transient blurred vision
cells.Diagnostics:
Clinical (scales on lashes + redness)
cornea/pupil/vision normal
cells.Treatment: Eyelid hygiene (baby shampoo/olive oil wipes, warm compress) ; topical antibiotics (erythro/bacitracin); oral doxy/tetracycline  if refractory
cells.Patient Education:
Lid hygiene (baby shampoo); avoid makeup until healed

Followup if lasts for weeks or severe redness, pain, vision changes or corneal involvement

cells.Definition / Overview: Bleeding under conjunctiva
cells.Clinical Presentation: Bright red patch, no pain/discharge, vision normal
cells.Patient Education: None

cells.Definition / Overview: Inflammation of conjunctiva (bacterial, viral, allergic)
cells.Etiology: Viral (adenovirus), bacterial (S. aureus, Strep, H. flu), allergic
cells.Diagnostics: Clinical + vision intact, corneal sensitivity normal
cells.Treatment:
Viral: supportive (cool compress + artificial tears)

Bacterial: topical antibiotics 

Allergic: avoid allergens antihistamine/decongestant drops
cells.Patient Education: Hand hygiene, no contacts/makeup, finish abx
cells.Complications: Herpetic keratitis (vision loss, decreased corneal density, herpetic lesions, unilateral)= EMERGENCY so referral

cells.Clinical Presentation: Severe pain, photophobia, FB sensation, tearing
cells.Treatment: Topical abx (erythro ointment); NSAIDs for pain; no steroids/anesthetics
cells.Patient Education:
Eye protection
URGENT FOLLOWUP IF NOT IMPROVED in 24-48 hours

cells.Clinical Presentation: Pain, tearing, FB sensation
cells.Treatment:
Remove (irrigation/swab), topical abx (erythromycin), urgent referral if deep
Remove within 24 hours
cells.Patient Education:
Eye protection
URGENT FOLLOWUP IF NOT IMPROVED in 24-48 hours

cells.Definition / Overview: Injury/infection from lens use
cells.Clinical Presentation: Dryness, pain, redness, abrasions and increased risk of infection
cells.Treatment: Stop lens; cold compress, NSAIDs; f/u daily x5 days
cells.Patient Education: No sleeping in contacts; replace lense/clean case regularly

cells.Definition / Overview: ↓ tear production or ↑ evaporation
cells.Clinical Presentation: Dry, gritty, burning eyes; FB sensation, blurred vision; paradoxical tearing, photophobia
cells.Patient Education:
Blink breaks, hydration, stop offending meds

Ophthalmology referral if neuropathy occurs

cells.Clinical Presentation: Redness, irritation, watery eye; vision intact
cells.Patient Education: Eye protection

cells.Clinical Presentation: Painless ↓ vision acuity, blurred/ hazy vision, halos, glare, difficulty driving at night
cells.Patient Education:
Sunglasses, referral
Management of diabetes

cells.Clinical Presentation: Pain, itching, drainage, hearing loss; pain with tragus palpation
cells.Treatment / Management: Debridement, irrigation, topical abx+steroid (Cipro HC, Cortisporin), pain control
cells.Patient Education: Ear hygiene, dry ears after water, avoid cotton swabs

cells.Etiology: S. pneumo, H. flu, M. catarrhalis, GAS, S. aureus
cells.Clinical Presentation: Ear pain, fever, irritability, drainage, ↓ hearing
cells.Treatment / Management: NSAIDs; Amox-clav 7–10d; alt: azithro/doxy; ENT if severe
cells.Patient Education: Adherence, follow-up

cells.Definition: Serous fluid in middle ear (not infected)
cells.Clinical Presentation: Ear fullness, hearing loss, popping, asymptomatic sometimes
cells.Treatment / Management: Watchful waiting; refer if >12 wks
cells.Patient Education: Monitor symptoms

cells.Definition: Abnormal skin growth in middle ear
cells.Etiology: Recurrent AOM, TM injury, bone anomalies
cells.Clinical Presentation: Hearing loss, recurrent infections, tinnitus, vertigo, purulent drainage
cells.Treatment / Management: Surgery (definitive), ENT referral
cells.Patient Education: Avoid recurrent infections

cells.Clinical Presentation: Fullness, ↓ hearing, tinnitus, dizziness
cells.Treatment / Management: Cerumenolytics, irrigation, curette
cells.Patient Education: Avoid cotton swabs; ear hygiene

cells.Definition:
Inflammation of pharynx/tonsils, acute or chronic; Most cases are viral & self-limited

Tonsillitis = acute/ chronic inflammation of tonsils, (viral or bacterial), similar presentation, diagnosis and management as pharyngitis
cells.Etiology: Viral (rhinovirus, EBV, influenza); Bacterial (GAS most common)
cells.Clinical Presentation:
Viral: URI sx (cough, congestion, conjunctivitis, hoarseness), low/no fever; pharyngeal edema, oral ulcers, viral exanthem 

Strep: NO URI sx, acute sore throat, fever (102-104), tonsillar exudates, pharyngeal erythema, palatal petechiae. strawberry tongue, scarlatiniform rash, tender nodes, no cough, N/V, abdomen pain
cells.Diagnostics:
Clinical Findings Strep Pharyngitis: red pharynx, uvula, tonsils, bilateral tonsillar exudates, tender cervical lymphadenopathy, petechia on soft palate, halitosis 

Viral: no test 

Bacterial: RADT; culture if negative esp children; ASO titers later
cells.Treatment / Management:
Viral: supportive (acetaminophen/NSAIDs, lozenges, fluids, humidification, voice rest, saline gargles)

Strep: penicillin/amox 10d (PCN allergy: clindamycin or clarithromycin 10d, azithromycin x 5d, macrolides)
cells.Patient Education:
Hand hygiene, replace toothbrush, no work/school 24h post-abx or until afebrile 

NO antibiotics in viral pharyngitis

cells.Definition: Pus collection between tonsil & constrictor muscle; deep neck infection
cells.Etiology:
Complication of tonsillitis (GAS)
Common in ages 20-40, increased risk with recurrent tonsillitis & smoking
cells.Clinical Presentation:
Fever, chills, malaise, halitosis, dysphagia, otalgia 
Severe sore throat, unilateral pain radiating to ear, trismus, “hot potato voice,” drooling
cells.Diagnostics:
Clinical= unilateral tonsil displaced medially downward, fluctuant peritonsillar tissue with erythema/ exudate, tender cervical nodes, trismus tachycardia drooling 

 CT w contrast (confirm abscess) /US if needed (bedside confirmation/ drainage guidance) 
CBC: leukocytosis 
Monospot (rule out mono)
cells.Treatment / Management: ENT referral; drainage + IV/PO abx (clindamycin, or  PCN+metro); steroids
cells.Patient Education: Hydration, med adherence

cells.Definition: Inflammation of epiglottis → airway obstruction → life threatening
cells.Etiology: Bacterial (Hib, strep, staph), viral, fungal, smoke inhalation
cells.Clinical Presentation: Abrupt rapidly progressive airway obstruction, sore throat, odynophagia, fever, dysphagia, drooling, tripod position, muffled voice, Neck tenderness, lymphadenopathy, respiratory distress
cells.Diagnostics:
Clinical; laryngoscopy with fiberoptic scope  (gold std, careful)

NO tongue depressors
cells.Treatment / Management:
IMMEDIATE ED/ENT 
Inpatient: urgent airway mgmt, IV abx
cells.Patient Education: Hib vaccine prevention; explain procedures, stress adherence, immunization status
cells.Complications: Death from airway obstruction (septicemia, meningitis, pulmonary edema, epiglottic abscess)

Triad: fever, lymphadenopathy, tonsillar pharyngitis

 Malaise, anorexia, atypical lymphocytosis, lympadenopathy ( posterior and cervical) splenomegaly, possible hepatomegaly, eyelid edema fatigue, rash possible
cells.Diagnostics: CBC (lymphocytosis, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia), Monospot, LFTs= ↑ AST/abnormal LFTs with pharyngitis
cells.Treatment / Management: Supportive (NSAIDs, fluids, rest); no abx
cells.Patient Education:
Avoid sports (splenic rupture risk), rest, hydration

Self-limited viral illness 
Teach comunicability
cells.Complications: Splenic rupture, airway obstruction, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly

cells.Definition/Overview: Acute inflammation of bronchi, usually viral, following URI; typically self-limiting; most common is viral infection (FLu, rhinovirus, covid, sars, rsv); can be bacterial
cells.Risk Factors: Recent URI, smoke/irritant exposure, allergens, chronic aspiration/GERD, undiagnosed asthma
cells.Clinical Features: Cough >5 days (1–3 wks), with or without sputum (clear/purulent), chest wall tenderness, nasal congestion, sore throat, possible wheeze/mild dyspnea, retrosternal pain during deep breathing and cough;  NO FEVER
cells.Diagnosis:
Clinical; Mildly elevated temp, pulse RR, O2 sat, few wheezes, pharynx may be injected; persistent cough for 1-3 weeks 
CXR only if pneumonia suspected
cells.Treatment/Management:
Supportive: rest, fluids, cough control , bronchodilators if wheeze; antibiotics not indicated in healthy individual

Avoid use of opioid cough suppressants, corticosteroids or herbal remedies
cells.Education/Prevention:
Hand hygiene, avoid smoke/irritants

Self limiting- it will improve (1-3 weeks) 

Return clinic if new onset fever, pleuritic chest pain. Difficulty breathing, bloody sputum, more than 4 weeks
cells.Complications/Referral: Refer if pneumonia suspected, hemoptysis, hypoxia, or symptoms >3 wks
cells.Differential Diagnosis: Allergic rhinitis, pneumonia, COVID 19, Influenza, Asthma, GERD, DRUGS, COPD/ emphysema, postnasal drip syndrome, Common cold, lung cancer

cells.Definition/Overview:
Chronic inflammatory airway disease with reversible obstruction & hyperresponsiveness characterized by wheezing breathlessness/dyspnea, chest tightness, coughing, particularly at night

Exacerbations:
Mild to moderate: talks in phrases, not agitated but tachypnic, NO accessory muscle use, O2 sat 90-95% 

Severe: talks in words, hunched forward, accessory muscles used, RR > 30, pulse > 120bpm, O sat < 90%
cells.Risk Factors: Atopy, Hx (wheeze, cough, SOB, chest tightness), allergens, infections, cold air, smoke, characteristic triggers (exercise,maybe pets)
cells.Clinical Features:
Episodic, recurrent wheeze, cough worse at night, chest tightness, dyspnea; worse at night/early AM; ↓ breath sounds if severe
Digital clubbing might occur -> sign of hypoxia
cells.Diagnosis:
Physical exam: wheezing on auscultation especially on expiration; confirmed with demonstration of variable expiratory airflow limitation, exclusion of alternative diagnosis 

Spirometry: ↓FEV1/FVC reversible post-bronchodilator (GOLD!)

peak expiratory flow(not diagnostic tho); FeNO if available
cells.Treatment/Management:
Stepwise: SABA → ICS → add LABA/↑ICS → LTRA/biologics; systemic steroids for exacerbations

Long-term control= inhaled corticosteroids, LABA, long acting antimuscarinic, methylaxanthines, leukotriene modifiers 

MART: use of ICS formoterol daily and as needed for symptoms 

Exacerbations:
Mild to moderate: SABA every 20 min x 1 hr, oral corticosteroid, controlled oxygen 

Severe: ER! SABA + ipra + O2 + oral corticosteroid 
911!!
cells.Education/Prevention:
Inhaler technique, trigger avoidance, action plan, vaccines

Followup: 
Gaining control: Every 2-6 wks
Monitor Control: 1-3 months
Step down: every 3 months
cells.Complications/Referral: Refer if severe/poor control; complications: status asthmaticus, airway remodeling; unresponsive to therapy after 3-6 months
cells.Differential Diagnosis: COPD, CHF, PE, Pneumonia, Cough secondary to ACE inhib, laryngeal dysfunction, benign and malignant tumors

cells.Definition/Overview:
Progressive, irreversible airflow limitation (chronic bronchitis + emphysema) occurs on most days for a minimum of 3 months a year for at least 2 successive years

Cough, dyspnea + airway limitation 
Preventable, treatable but NOT reversible
cells.Risk Factors: Smoking, occupational exposures, structural changes of the lung caused by childhood pneumonia, TB, HIV, premie, early life asthma, COPD FHx
cells.Clinical Features:
Chronic cough, sputum production (colorless sputum worse in morning), dyspnea, 

Less common= wheeze/ chest tightness, difficulty speaking/ performing tasks, weight loss, weight gain, limitation of activity (sex), depression/anxiety 

exacerbations = worse dyspnea/sputum/cough, could become hypoxic
cells.Diagnosis:
Suggestive: Hx of symptoms + exposure + fam hx of chronic lung disease + comorbidities 

Confirmation: Spirometry (gold standard): FEV1/FVC <0.70 post-BD + exclusion of alt diagnosis 

GOLD 1 (mild disease): FEV > 80 percent predicted 
GOLD 2 (moderate disease): FEV1 between 50 and 80 percent predicted 
GOLD 3 (severe disease) FEV1 between 30 and 50 percent predicted 
GOLD 4 (very severe disease): FEV < 30 percent predicted
cells.Treatment/Management:
Smoking cessation, bronchodilators (SABA/LABA/LAMA), ICS if frequent exacerbations, oxygen if hypoxemic, pulm rehab

Exacerbation Tx = Prednisone for 5-14 days + smoking cessation + physical activity + low carb diet + antibiotics if bacterial infection
cells.Education/Prevention:
Quit smoking, vaccines (flu and pneumo and COVID), rehab

Repeat spirometry annually 

Anticipatory guidance for sexual dysfunction 

Educate on inhalers
cells.Complications/Referral: Refer for frequent exacerbations or oxygen need; complications: cor pulmonale, resp failure
cells.Differential Diagnosis: Chronic obstructive asthma, chronic bronchitis with normal spirometry, bronchiectasis, HF, TB, pneumonia

cells.Definition/Overview:
Acute infection of lung parenchyma acquired outside hospital/LTC
Can be bacterial, atypical bacteria, or viral= most common bacterial is S. pneumoniae
cells.Risk Factors: Age extremes, COPD/DM/HF, smoking, immunosuppression, low income, crowded living condition
cells.Clinical Features: Cough, fever, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, purulent sputum; rales, egophony, dullness
cells.Diagnosis:
CXR: lobar infiltrate/consolidation via Chest Xray (first line; gold standard) or CT scan (second); sputum/blood cultures if severe; CURB-65 for severity, CBC with differential 

CURB-65 = new onset confusion, BUN > 20, RR > 30, BP < 90/60, Age > 65
cells.Treatment/Management:
Healthy+ no abx use/allergies= amoxicillin+ doxy, or macrolide 

Comorbidities = Augmentin + doxy or maco 

PCN allergy = 3 gen cephalosporin + macro or doxy 

COPD/ unable to take cephalosporins = respiratory fluoroquinolones
cells.Education/Prevention:
Complete antibiotics, hydration, vaccines (flu, pneumo, COVID)

SMOKING CESSATION + FLU VAC + PNEUMO VAC 

No followup imaging typically required
cells.Complications/Referral: Admit if hypoxic/unstable/multilobar or CURB-65 ≥2; complications: empyema, sepsis, resp failure
cells.Differential Diagnosis: PE, CHF w pulmonary edema, atelectasis, lung cancer, bronchiectasis, spiration/ chemical pneumonitis, drug reaction, asthma/COPD, acute bronchitis, influenza and respiratory virus

cells.Definition/Overview:
Chronic M. tuberculosis infection; latent or active, may involve lungs, liver , spleen, kidney, brain and bone.
Most common HIV opportunistic infection
cells.Risk Factors: TB contact, immunosuppressed (HIV/steroids), close quarters, foreign-born, homeless, incarcerated, drug use/ alcoholism, steroid therapy, cancer chemo, hematologic malignancies
cells.Clinical Features:
Active: chronic cough, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, weight loss/ difficulty gaining weight; chills, hemoptysis, fatigue 

Latent: asymptomatic
cells.Diagnosis:
Purified Protein Derivative (PDD) testing, CXR (apical lesions); sputum AFB smear/culture = gold standard,  gastric aspirate culture, MRI, CBC with differential CRP 
Mantoux Tuberculin Skin test 

Definitive diagnosis = isolation of M. tuberculosis from a bodily secretion or tissue
cells.Treatment/Management:
Latent: INH 6–9 mo or rifampin 4 mo; 

Active: RIPE (rifampin, INH, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) 2 mo → INH + rifampin 4 mo
cells.Education/Prevention:
Adherence, DOT, isolation if active, reportable disease to state and local health department, monitor liver function 

Regular f/u every 4-8 weeks to ensure compliance, monitor adverse effects of medications 

Repeat CXR after 2-3 months to evaluate response to treatment
cells.Complications/Referral: Refer to TB specialist; complications: miliary TB, meningitis, MDR-TB
cells.Differential Diagnosis: Asthma, malignancies, aspiration pneumonia, bronchiectasis, pleurist, histoplasmosis, silicosis, COPD

cells.Definition/Overview: Malignant lung tumor (NSCLC vs SCLC); leading cause of cancer death
cells.Risk Factors: Smoking!!!, asbestos, radon, FHx
cells.Clinical Features: Cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, dyspnea, chest pain, recurrent pneumonia, hoarseness; paraneoplastic syndromes
cells.Diagnosis:
CXR/CT mass; bronchoscopy with biopsy; staging with CT/PET/MRI
Definitive diagnosis requires cytologic or histologic evidence
cells.Treatment/Management: NSCLC: surgery if localized ± chemo/radiation; SCLC: chemo + radiation; targeted/immunotherapy as indicated
cells.Education/Prevention: Smoking cessation; screening 50-80: annual low-dose CT age 50–80 with ≥20 pack-years, current smoker or quit <15 yrs
cells.Complications/Referral: Refer to oncology; complications: brain, bone, liver mets, malignant effusion

cells.Definition / Epidemiology: Excess thyroid hormone production or release; affects multiple systems
cells.Causes / Types: Primary (thyroid origin, ↓TSH) Secondary (pituitary, ↑TSH) Tertiary (hypothalamus, ↑TRH) Causes: Graves’ disease (MC), toxic adenoma, multinodular goiter (Plummer’s), thyroiditis (subacute painful, silent, postpartum), struma ovarii, excess thyroid hormone, TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, thyroid hormone resistance, hCG tumors, gestational thyrotoxicosis
cells.Clinical Features: • Nervousness, tremor, palpitations, heat intolerance • Weight loss despite ↑ appetite • Goiter, tachycardia, AFib • Graves’: ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxedema
cells.Diagnostics: Labs: TSH (best screen ↓), Free T4/T3 ↑ Imaging: Radioiodine uptake (diffuse in Graves’, focal in nodules), MRI if suspicious nodules
cells.Management: Symptomatic: Beta-blockers (propranolol, atenolol) Thioamides: Methimazole (preferred), PTU (pregnancy/1st trimester) Radioiodine ablation: >20 yrs, failed meds, contraindicated in pregnancy & ophthalmopathy Surgery: if obstructive goiter, pregnancy intolerant to meds, RAI refusal
cells.Complications / Education: Complications: Untreated → AFib, CHF, angina, osteoporosis Thyroid storm: fever, tachy, AFib, delirium, GI symptoms (emergency) Education: monitor HR, signs of agranulocytosis on thioamides, adherence, possible hypothyroidism post-therapy

cells.Definition / Epidemiology: Inadequate thyroid hormone production; ~4.6% U.S. prevalence; 5–8x more common in women; compromises nearly all body systems
cells.Causes / Types: Primary (MC): thyroid disease (Hashimoto’s MC in US) Central: pituitary or hypothalamic failure Iatrogenic: thyroidectomy, RAI, external radiation, meds (lithium, amiodarone, interferon) Congenital: thyroid dysgenesis, iodine deficiency, maternal antibodies Transient: postpartum thyroiditis, subacute thyroiditis Subclinical: ↑TSH, normal T4 (risk CVD, infertility, neuro symptoms)
cells.Clinical Features: • Fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance • Constipation, hoarseness, slow thinking • Dry skin, brittle hair • Bradycardia • Myxedema: puffiness, periorbital edema, slow reflexes
cells.Diagnostics: Labs: TSH (high in primary; low/normal in central), Free T4 low Antimicrosomal/anti-TPO antibodies (Hashimoto’s) Ultrasound, FNAC if suspicious nodules
cells.Management: Replacement: Levothyroxine (T4) 1.6–1.7 mcg/kg/day Start low in elderly/heart disease (12.5–25 mcg) Monitor TSH every 6 wks; adjust 12.5–25 mcg Subclinical: treat if TSH ≥10 or symptomatic Hashimoto’s: lifelong levothyroxine
cells.Complications / Education: Complications: Myxedema coma (severe, emergency; ↓ mental status, hypothermia, organ failure) Risk factors: untreated hypo, infection, cold, MI, surgery, sedatives Education: lifelong meds, take in AM, avoid interfering meds (iron, calcium, sucralfate, TFs), dosing changes in illness/pregnancy, avoid substitutions

cells.Definition / Epidemiology: Most common endocrine cancer; ~57k new cases/yr (2017); 3x more in women; usually slow-growing; MC age 20–54; RF: ionizing radiation
cells.Causes / Types: Differentiated: Papillary (MC, ~60%), Follicular Undifferentiated: Medullary (familial, MEN2), Anaplastic (aggressive, iodine-deficient regions)
cells.Clinical Features: • Painless lump/nodule (MC symptom) • Neck fullness, dysphagia, SOB • New hoarseness (highly suspicious) • Hemoptysis, lymphadenopathy • Neck pain (late)
cells.Diagnostics: Labs: TSH usually normal (used for monitoring post-treatment) Ultrasound: detects nodules but not malignant vs benign RAI uptake: + uptake favorable prognosis US-guided FNA: gold standard (83% sens, 92% spec) CT/MRI: for large/recurrent tumors, metastasis
cells.Management: Management: Endocrinology referral TSH suppression with high-dose thyroxine Thyroidectomy (± lymph node clearance) Radiation therapy (regional or total body) ± Chemotherapy Multidisciplinary approach
cells.Complications / Education: Education: Monthly neck checks if family hx, goiter hx, or prior radiation Teach self-check safely Stress early evaluation of new lumps/hoarseness

cells.Notes: Most common form; Hashimoto’s, iatrogenic, iodine deficiency
Early hypo; risk of CVD, infertility; may progress
Often multinodular goiter or nodules; ↑ AFib risk
Rare; tissues resistant to thyroid hormone
TFTs not diagnostic; TSH used to monitor treatment response

cells.Key Features / Presentation: Recurrent attacks (4 phases: prodrome, aura, headache, postdrome). POUND: Pulsatile, One-day duration, Unilateral, Nausea/vomiting, Disabling.
cells.Diagnostics / Work-up: Clinical dx; no imaging if stable & meets criteria. Labs: CBC, ESR, TSH, Lyme, RF if suspicious. Imaging (CT/MRI) if red flags (SNOOP10).
cells.Treatment / Management: Abortive: NSAIDs, acetaminophen, triptans (e.g., sumatriptan, rizatriptan), antiemetics. Preventive: propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate, valproate, CGRP antagonists. Non-pharm: relaxation, CBT, biofeedback.
cells.Differentials: Tension headache, cluster, sinus, tumor, hemorrhage, aneurysm, thyroid issues, sleep apnea.

cells.Key Features / Presentation: Bilateral, pressing/tightening, mild-moderate, not worsened by activity. No N/V, no photophobia/phonophobia. Triggered by stress, posture.
cells.Treatment / Management: Acute: NSAIDs, aspirin ± caffeine. Preventive: amitriptyline, venlafaxine; biofeedback, acupuncture, relaxation, botulinum toxin.
cells.Differentials: Migraine, sinus HA, TMJ, arthritis, MOH, brain tumor.

cells.Key Features / Presentation: Severe unilateral orbital/temporal pain with autonomic features (tearing, rhinorrhea, congestion, sweating, ptosis, miosis). More common in men. Restlessness.
cells.Diagnostics / Work-up: Neuroimaging recommended to r/o secondary causes.
cells.Treatment / Management: Acute: 100% O₂, subq sumatriptan. Preventive: verapamil (high dose), glucocorticoids during initiation, topiramate, nerve blocks if refractory.

cells.Key Features / Presentation: Headaches worsened by frequent analgesic use.
cells.Diagnostics / Work-up: History of med use. Thresholds: NSAIDs ≥15d/mo; triptans/ergots ≥10d/mo; combo analgesics ≥10d/mo.
cells.Treatment / Management: Discontinue overused meds. Start preventive therapy (topiramate, beta-blocker, CGRP). Education critical.

cells.Key Features / Presentation: Acute unilateral peripheral facial paralysis, peaks in 72h. Smooth forehead, mouth droop, tearing, tinnitus, hyperacusis. RF: DM, pregnancy, hypothyroid, URI.
cells.Diagnostics / Work-up: Clinical dx. Lyme titer if risk. Imaging if atypical/bilateral. Use House-Brackmann scale.
cells.Treatment / Management: Prednisone 60mg ×5d ± acyclovir. Eye care: lubricants, glasses, tape at night. Refer if atypical.
cells.Differentials: Stroke (forehead sparing), tumor, MS, Lyme, Guillain-Barré, otitis media, Ramsay Hunt.

cells.Key Features / Presentation: Vertigo: spinning, vestibular cause. Presyncope: lightheaded, CV cause. Disequilibrium: imbalance, cerebellar/peripheral neuropathy. Non-specific: vague, meds/anxiety.
cells.Diagnostics / Work-up: TiTrATE: Timing, Triggers, Targeted exam. Dix-Hallpike (BPPV), orthostatics, EKG if presyncope, audiometry if hearing loss, imaging if neuro deficits.
cells.Treatment / Management: BPPV → Epley maneuver. Vestibular rehab. Antiemetics short-term. Refer if unclear.
cells.Differentials: BPPV, vestibular neuritis, central stroke, arrhythmia, neuropathy, metabolic, anxiety.

cells.Key Features / Presentation: Dermatomal painful vesicular rash preceded by tingling. Post-herpetic neuralgia possible.
cells.Treatment / Management: Antivirals: valacyclovir, acyclovir (within 72h). Prednisone for acute pain. PHN: gabapentin, pregabalin. Vaccine: Shingrix ≥50yo.

cells.Key Features / Presentation: Transient excessive electrical brain activity. Post-ictal confusion common.
cells.Diagnostics / Work-up: Clinical history, witness report. Work-up: r/o metabolic, trauma, infection, stroke.
cells.Treatment / Management: AEDs (antiepileptic drugs), seizure precautions, lifestyle modification.
cells.Differentials: Syncope, arrhythmia, TIA, migraine, tumor, hypoglycemia, psychogenic non-epileptic seizures.

cells.Key Features / Presentation: Tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability. Fall risk, mood/sleep issues, constipation, sialorrhea.
cells.Diagnostics / Work-up: Clinical dx. Exclude atypical features (symmetry, rapid progression, early falls).
cells.Treatment / Management: Levodopa, dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors. Non-pharm: exercise, PT/OT. Support caregiver.
cells.Differentials: Essential tremor, drug-induced parkinsonism, atypical parkinsonism.

cells.Key Features / Presentation: Chronic autoimmune CNS inflammation. Symptoms: optic neuritis, paresthesias, weakness, fatigue.
cells.Diagnostics / Work-up: MRI brain/spine, CSF oligoclonal bands, exclude mimics (B12 deficiency, Lyme).
cells.Treatment / Management: Disease-modifying therapies (DMTs), steroids for relapses, rehab.

cells.Key Features / Presentation: Memory loss, impaired language, behavior/personality changes. Alzheimer’s most common.
cells.Diagnostics / Work-up: MoCA/MMSE, labs (TSH, B12, CMP, CBC), neuroimaging if atypical.
cells.Treatment / Management: Supportive care, cholinesterase inhibitors, memantine, caregiver support.

cells.Key Features / Presentation: Chronic widespread pain ≥3mo, fatigue, sleep disturbance, cognitive symptoms. WPI ≥7 + SSS ≥5 (or WPI 4–6 + SSS ≥9).
cells.Diagnostics / Work-up: Rule out mimics (TSH, ESR, CRP). Clinical dx.
cells.Treatment / Management: Non-pharm: exercise, CBT, sleep hygiene. Pharm: duloxetine, milnacipran, pregabalin, low-dose amitriptyline.

cells.Key Features / Presentation: Numbness, tingling, burning pain. Common in diabetes.
cells.Treatment / Management: Manage cause, TCAs, anticonvulsants, pain referral.

cells.Key Features / Presentation: Sudden neuro deficit: weakness, numbness, aphasia, vision loss, severe headache.
cells.Diagnostics / Work-up: NIH Stroke Scale. Imaging (CT/MRI), labs (CBC, CMP, coag).
cells.Treatment / Management: Ischemic: thrombolytics (if eligible), thrombectomy. Hemorrhagic: BP control, neurosurgery. Long-term: secondary prevention.
cells.Differentials: Migraine, seizure, tumor, hypoglycemia, panic attack, conversion disorder.

cells.Key Features / Presentation: Fever, headache, stiff neck, photophobia, AMS. RF: HIV, sickle cell, asplenia, EtOH.
cells.Diagnostics / Work-up: CBC, LP with CSF analysis, CT if ICP ↑ suspected.
cells.Treatment / Management: IV antibiotics (don’t delay if toxic), vaccines (MCV4, MPSV4, pneumococcal).

cells.Key Features / Presentation: Acute fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition. Hours–days onset.
cells.Diagnostics / Work-up: CAM tool (acute onset + inattention + [disorganized thinking or altered consciousness]). Work-up: CBC, BMP, TSH, UA, tox screen, imaging if unclear.
cells.Treatment / Management: Treat underlying cause, reorientation, avoid sedatives, supportive care.

cells.Overview: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) results from plaque buildup; prevention is key.
cells.Risk Factors: Non-modifiable: Age, sex, family history.Modifiable: Smoking, dyslipidemia, DM, obesity, inactivity, poor diet, HTN, stress.
cells.Key Diagnostics: ASCVD risk calculator (10-year risk, ages 40–79).CAC scoring for selected patients.
cells.Clinical Features: Often silent until MI, stroke, or PAD.
cells.Management/Treatment: Lifestyle modification: diet (DASH/Mediterranean), exercise ≥150 min/week, weight loss, BP, lipid & DM control, smoking cessation.
cells.Patient Education/Prevention: Avoid refined carbs, sugars, processed meats, trans fats. Avoid vaping.
cells.Referral/Complications: Refer if high ASCVD risk or resistant HTN/DM. Complications: MI, stroke, PAD, sudden cardiac death.

cells.Overview: Chronic elevation of BP, leading to vascular damage and end-organ disease.
cells.Risk Factors: Non-modifiable: Age, CKD, family history, male sex.Modifiable: Obesity, DM, inactivity, OSA, alcohol, high sodium, smoking.
cells.Key Diagnostics: BP ≥130/80 (multiple visits).Labs: CMP, CBC, lipids, TSH, UA.EKG, echo, renal US if secondary.
cells.Clinical Features: Often asymptomatic; may cause HA, dizziness, vision changes, chest pain, dyspnea.
cells.Management/Treatment: Lifestyle: weight loss, ↓Na+, DASH diet, exercise, ↓ETOH.Pharm: Thiazide, ACE/ARB, CCB, BB (with comorbid).Resistant → add spironolactone.
cells.Referral/Complications: Refer resistant HTN or secondary suspicion. Complications: MI, stroke, HF, CKD, aneurysm, retinopathy. Hospitalize hypertensive emergency.

cells.Overview: Atherosclerotic obstruction of coronary arteries → angina, MI.
cells.Risk Factors: Same ASCVD risks: smoking, DM, HTN, dyslipidemia, age, family history.
cells.Key Diagnostics: ECG, stress test (exercise/nuclear/echo), coronary CT/MRI, angiography (gold standard).
cells.Clinical Features: Angina (chest pressure radiating to arm/jaw), SOB, fatigue, atypical sx in women.
cells.Management/Treatment: Lifestyle changes, ASA, statins, BB, ACE/ARB, nitrates, CCB, antiplatelets. Cardiac rehab.
cells.Referral/Complications: Refer new angina, abnormal ECG/stress, suspected ACS. Complications: MI, arrhythmias, HF, sudden death.

cells.Overview: Supraventricular arrhythmia with irregularly irregular rhythm; ↑ stroke risk.
cells.Risk Factors: Age, HTN, CAD, HF, valve disease, thyroid disease, obesity, alcohol.
cells.Key Diagnostics: ECG (no P waves, irregular RR), Holter monitor, TSH. CHA₂DS₂-VASc for stroke risk.
cells.Clinical Features: Palpitations, SOB, fatigue, dizziness, syncope, or asymptomatic.
cells.Management/Treatment: Rate control: BB, CCB, digoxin.Rhythm control: cardioversion, antiarrhythmics.Anticoagulation: NOACs, warfarin.
cells.Patient Education/Prevention: Avoid alcohol, caffeine, stimulants. Monitor HR and sx.
cells.Referral/Complications: Refer new AFib, refractory, symptomatic. Hospitalize unstable cases. Complications: stroke, HF, embolism.

cells.Risk Factors: Rheumatic fever, IV drug use, congenital disease, age-related degeneration.
cells.Key Diagnostics: New murmur, echo (gold standard), cardiac MRI.
cells.Clinical Features: DOE, chest pain, syncope, HF sx, murmur.
cells.Management/Treatment: GDMT for HF sx, surgical repair/replacement for severe disease.
cells.Patient Education/Prevention: Dental hygiene, med adherence, avoid IV drug use.
cells.Referral/Complications: Refer new murmur, symptomatic, severe VHD. Hospitalize if unstable. Complications: HF, arrhythmia, sudden death.

cells.Overview: Syndrome of impaired ventricular filling (HFpEF) or ejection (HFrEF).
cells.Risk Factors: HTN, CAD, DM, obesity, AFib, OSA, valve disease.
cells.Management/Treatment: HFrEF: ARNI/ACE/ARB, BB, aldosterone antagonist, SGLT2i, diuretics.HFpEF: risk factor control, diuretics, BP mgmt.
cells.Patient Education/Prevention: Daily weights, sodium restriction, med adherence.
cells.Referral/Complications: Refer new or moderate-severe, unclear etiology, refractory. Hospitalize decompensated HF. Complications: arrhythmia, renal failure, sudden death.

cells.Overview: PAD = arterial narrowing of extremities; Venous = chronic insufficiency.
cells.Risk Factors: Smoking, DM, dyslipidemia, HTN, obesity, inactivity, age.
cells.Clinical Features: PAD: intermittent claudication, wounds.Venous: edema, varicosities, leg aches, skin changes.
cells.Management/Treatment: PAD: smoking cessation, statins, antiplatelets, supervised exercise, revascularization.Venous: compression stockings, leg elevation, exercise.
cells.Patient Education/Prevention: Foot care, smoking cessation, exercise, compression stockings.
cells.Referral/Complications: Refer critical limb ischemia, ulcers, severe sx. Complications: gangrene, amputation, venous ulcers, DVT.

cells.What it is: Atherosclerotic narrowing of lower extremity arteries
cells.Risk Factors: Smoking, DM, HTN, HLD, obesity, age ≥65, FHx CVD
cells.Clinical Presentation: Intermittent claudication, rest pain, ulcers, gangrene, dependent rubor, trophic changes
cells.Management (Non-Pharm + Pharm): Lifestyle: smoking cessation, exercise therapy, foot care.Pharm: Statins (↓ LDL <70), Antiplatelets (ASA, clopidogrel), Cilostazol (improves claudication; avoid in HF).Procedures: angioplasty/stenting, bypass for critical limb ischemia.

cells.Risk Factors: HTN, HLD, DM, smoking
cells.Clinical Presentation: Often silent; may present with TIA/stroke sx (weakness, speech, vision loss)
cells.Management (Non-Pharm + Pharm): Lifestyle: smoking cessation, diet/exercise.Pharm: Statins (LDL <70), Antiplatelets (ASA, clopidogrel), Antihypertensives (ACEi/ARB, BB, thiazides).Surgery: Carotid endarterectomy/stenting if ≥50% symptomatic or ≥70% asymptomatic.

cells.What it is: Dilation of thoracic aorta (ascending, arch, descending)
cells.Risk Factors: Genetic syndromes, bicuspid AV, HTN, smoking
cells.Clinical Presentation: Often asymptomatic; may cause chest/back pain, compressive sx
cells.Management (Non-Pharm + Pharm): Lifestyle: smoking cessation, risk factor control.Pharm: BP control with Beta-blockers (↓ wall stress), ARBs (esp. Marfan/Loeys-Dietz). Statins.Surgery: repair if ≥5.5 cm or rapid growth.

cells.Risk Factors: Smoking, male sex, HTN, age, FHx, COPD
cells.Clinical Presentation: Often asymptomatic; pulsatile abdominal mass; rupture = hypotension, shock
cells.Management (Non-Pharm + Pharm): Lifestyle: smoking cessation.Pharm: Statins, Antihypertensives (esp. BB, ACE/ARB).Surgery: repair if >5.0–5.5 cm, symptomatic, or enlarging.

cells.Risk Factors: HTN, connective tissue disorders, bicuspid AV, cocaine
cells.Clinical Presentation: Sudden severe chest/back pain, shock, neuro deficits
cells.Management (Non-Pharm + Pharm): Acute Rx: IV Beta-blockers (labetalol, esmolol) for HR/BP control; add vasodilators (nitroprusside) after BB.Type A: emergent surgery.Type B: medical therapy unless unstable → TEVAR.

cells.Risk Factors: Virchow’s triad (stasis, injury, hypercoag), malignancy, surgery, OCP, pregnancy
cells.Clinical Presentation: Unilateral swelling, pain, warmth, erythema
cells.Management (Non-Pharm + Pharm): Lifestyle: ambulation, compression stockings.Pharm: Anticoagulation (DOACs [apixaban, rivaroxaban], LMWH, warfarin). Thrombolysis (tPA) if massive iliofemoral DVT.

cells.What it is: Thrombus in superficial veins (saphenous, cephalic, basilic)
cells.Risk Factors: Varicosities, IV catheters, trauma, malignancy
cells.Clinical Presentation: Palpable cord, erythema, tenderness
cells.Management (Non-Pharm + Pharm): Lifestyle: leg elevation, warm compress, compression stockings.Pharm: Anticoagulation (fondaparinux, LMWH, DOAC) if >5 cm or near deep system. NSAIDs for pain.

cells.What it is: Embolus (usually from DVT) in pulmonary arteries
cells.Risk Factors: Same as DVT
cells.Clinical Presentation: Dyspnea, chest pain, tachycardia, hemoptysis, syncope
cells.Management (Non-Pharm + Pharm): Pharm: Anticoagulation (DOACs, LMWH, warfarin). Thrombolysis (tPA) if massive/submassive PE. IV heparin bridge if unstable.

cells.Risk Factors: Pregnancy, obesity, prolonged standing, DVT hx, FHx
cells.Clinical Presentation: Leg edema, varicosities, hyperpigmentation, venous stasis ulcers
cells.Management (Non-Pharm + Pharm): Lifestyle: leg elevation, weight loss, exercise, compression stockings.Pharm: Venoactive drugs (micronized flavonoids – not FDA standard). Anticoagulation not routine unless DVT hx.Procedures: endovenous ablation, sclerotherapy, phlebectomy.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Periumbilical → RLQ pain (McBurney’s), fever, N/V, rebound, guarding.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Surgical referral; IV Ceftriaxone 1 g + Metronidazole 500 mg pre-op.
cells.Patient Education: Seek emergency care for fever/worsening pain; NPO until evaluated.

cells.Clinical Presentation: RUQ pain radiating to shoulder, fever, Murphy’s sign.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily + Metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h; surgery.
cells.Patient Education: Avoid fatty meals; return if fever/chills.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Severe diffuse abdominal pain, rigid abdomen, rebound, fever.
cells.Diagnostics: CBC, CMP, CT abdomen with contrast.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Broad-spectrum IV abx (Piperacillin–Tazobactam 3.375 g q6h)**; surgical emergency.
cells.Patient Education: Medical emergency—do not eat/drink; seek immediate care.

cells.Definition: Pancreatic inflammation from gallstones or alcohol.
cells.Clinical Presentation: Sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to back; N/V; worse supine.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Lactated Ringer’s 250–500 mL/hr, Morphine 2–4 mg IV, NPO.
cells.Patient Education: Avoid alcohol; low-fat diet after recovery.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Chronic epigastric pain, steatorrhea, weight loss.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Pancrelipase with meals, analgesics.
cells.Patient Education: Low-fat diet; avoid alcohol strictly.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Straining, bloating.
cells.Diagnostics: Rule out obstruction; TSH if chronic.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Polyethylene glycol 17 g daily, Senna 8.6 mg HS.
cells.Patient Education: Increase water, fiber, activity.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Hematemesis, melena, dizziness.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Pantoprazole 80 mg IV bolus → 8 mg/hr infusion.
cells.Patient Education: Report black stools or vomiting blood immediately.

cells.Definition: Bleeding from colon, rectum, hemorrhoids, etc.
cells.Clinical Presentation: Bright red blood, rectal pain or none.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Treat cause: hemorrhoids—hydrocortisone suppository; diverticular bleed—ER referral.
cells.Patient Education: Increase fiber; report heavy bleeding.

cells.Definition: Reflux of stomach acid into esophagus.
cells.Clinical Presentation: Heartburn, regurgitation, chronic cough.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Omeprazole 20–40 mg daily x 4–8 weeks.
cells.Patient Education: Avoid trigger foods, late meals, elevate HOB.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Burning epigastric pain; duodenal improves w/ food.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): PPI: Omeprazole 20–40 mg daily; if H. pylori positive → triple therapy.
cells.Patient Education: Avoid NSAIDs, alcohol; complete antibiotic regimen.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Epigastric pain, nausea, bloating.
cells.Diagnostics: Stool antigen or urea breath test.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Triple Therapy x14 days: Omeprazole 20 mg BID + Amoxicillin 1 g BID + Clarithromycin 500 mg BID.
cells.Patient Education: Retest 4 weeks post-treatment; no PPIs 2 weeks before retesting.

cells.Definition: Autoimmune gluten intolerance causing villous atrophy.
cells.Clinical Presentation: Diarrhea, bloating, weight loss, dermatitis herpetiformis.
cells.Diagnostics: tTG-IgA, EMA antibodies, small bowel biopsy.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Strict gluten-free diet.
cells.Patient Education: Avoid wheat, barley, rye; check labels for hidden gluten.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Abdominal pain + change in stool (constipation, diarrhea, or mixed).
cells.Diagnostics: Rome IV criteria; normal labs; colonoscopy if red flags.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): IBS-C: Linaclotide 145 mcg daily. IBS-D: Loperamide 2–4 mg PRN, Dicyclomine 20 mg QID.
cells.Patient Education: Low FODMAP diet; stress management; fiber supplementation for IBS-C.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Bloody diarrhea (UC), RLQ pain (Crohn’s), weight loss.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Mesalamine 2.4–4.8 g/day (UC), Budesonide 9 mg/day (Crohn’s), biologics (Adalimumab) if severe.
cells.Patient Education: Avoid NSAIDs; monitor for dehydration; smoking cessation (Crohn’s improved).

cells.Clinical Presentation: Usually asymptomatic; may have painless rectal bleeding.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Increase fiber 20–30 g/day.
cells.Patient Education: Hydration; fiber daily.

cells.Clinical Presentation: LLQ pain, fever, N/V.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg BID x 7–10 days OR Cipro 500 mg BID + Metronidazole 500 mg TID.
cells.Patient Education: Clear liquids 24–48 hr then advance diet; return if fever/worsening pain.

sections.title: GI Infections, Liver disorders, GI cancers

cells.Clinical Presentation: N/V/D, cramps, low-grade fever.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Oral rehydration, Ondansetron 4 mg ODT q8h PRN.
cells.Patient Education: Hydration; handwashing; avoid dairy temporarily.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Bloody diarrhea (E. coli, Shigella), fever.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Avoid antibiotics in O157:H7; others: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BID x 3 days.
cells.Patient Education: Avoid high-risk foods; hydration.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Fever, fatigue, jaundice, RUQ pain.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Supportive only.
cells.Patient Education: Vaccination; avoid alcohol.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Fatigue, jaundice, dark urine.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Tenofovir 300 mg daily for chronic infection.
cells.Patient Education: Safe sex, vaccinate close contacts, avoid alcohol.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Often asymptomatic; chronic liver disease.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Epclusa (sofosbuvir/velpatasvir) 1 tab daily x 12 wks.
cells.Patient Education: Avoid alcohol; screen for cirrhosis; safe sex.

cells.Definition: D requires HBV; E fecal-oral (pregnancy risk).
cells.Clinical Presentation: Acute hepatitis symptoms.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Supportive.
cells.Patient Education: Vaccinate against HBV (prevents HDV).

cells.Clinical Presentation: Usually asymptomatic; RUQ discomfort.
cells.Diagnostics: Elevated ALT>AST; ultrasound shows fatty liver.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Weight loss (7–10%), control DM/lipids; Vitamin E 800 IU/day (non-diabetic).
cells.Patient Education: Avoid alcohol; Mediterranean diet; exercise.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Progressive dysphagia, weight loss.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Oncology referral; surgery/chemo/radiation.
cells.Patient Education: Avoid smoking/alcohol; report swallowing trouble early.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Early satiety, weight loss, epigastric pain.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Oncology referral.
cells.Patient Education: H. pylori eradication reduces risk.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Change in stool, blood in stool, anemia, weight loss.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Surgical resection + oncology.
cells.Patient Education: Screening starting at 45; family history screening earlier.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Painless jaundice, weight loss, back pain.
cells.Treatment (Specific Meds/Doses): Oncology referral.
cells.Patient Education: Avoid smoking; genetic screening if family history.

cells.Definition: Malignant tumor of the testicle, usually germ-cell.
cells.Clinical Presentation: Painless unilateral testicular mass; heaviness; sometimes gynecomastia.
cells.Diagnostics: Scrotal ultrasound (solid mass), AFP, β-hCG, LDH, CT pelvis/abdomen.
cells.Treatment (Specific Drugs/Doses When App: Urgent urology referral; orchiectomy. Chemo based on staging (cisplatin-based).
cells.Patient Education: Monthly testicular exams; excellent cure rate; importance of follow-up imaging.

cells.Definition: Twisting of spermatic cord → ischemia. Surgical emergency.
cells.Clinical Presentation: Sudden severe unilateral pain, high-riding testicle, absent cremasteric reflex.
cells.Diagnostics: Doppler ultrasound (decreased flow). Clinical dx if high suspicion.
cells.Patient Education: Come to ED within hours of pain; fertility risk if delayed.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Painless scrotal swelling; transilluminates.
cells.Diagnostics: Physical exam; scrotal ultrasound if unclear.
cells.Treatment (Specific Drugs/Doses When App: Observation if asymptomatic; surgical repair if large/symptomatic.
cells.Patient Education: Usually benign; monitor for size changes.

cells.Definition: Dilation of pampiniform plexus (“bag of worms”).
cells.Clinical Presentation: Dull ache; worse standing; left-sided > right.
cells.Treatment (Specific Drugs/Doses When App: Spermatic vein ligation or embolization if infertility/pain.
cells.Patient Education: Improves fertility; avoid prolonged standing.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Smooth, painless, cystic mass superior to testicle.
cells.Patient Education: Usually harmless; report enlarging masses.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Gradual onset scrotal pain, + Prehn sign (relief w/ elevation), dysuria, fever.
cells.Diagnostics: UA, urine culture; test for GC/CT (NAAT); scrotal US if needed.
cells.Treatment (Specific Drugs/Doses When App: Age <35 (likely GC/CT): Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once + Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID × 7 days. Age >35 (likely E. coli): Levofloxacin 500 mg PO daily × 10 days.
cells.Patient Education: Scrotal support; avoid intercourse until treated; finish all antibiotics.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Testicular pain/swelling; fever; in mumps: parotitis.
cells.Diagnostics: Clinical; ultrasound to rule out torsion.
cells.Treatment (Specific Drugs/Doses When App: Viral: supportive. Bacterial: treat as epididymitis.
cells.Patient Education: MMR vaccine prevents mumps orchitis; supportive care.

cells.Definition: Blood in tunica vaginalis, usually trauma-related.
cells.Clinical Presentation: Painful swelling; does not transilluminate.
cells.Treatment (Specific Drugs/Doses When App: Rest, scrotal support; large cases → surgical drainage.
cells.Patient Education: Safety with sports; seek care for any testicular trauma.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Urinary hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia, incomplete emptying.
cells.Diagnostics: DRE, PSA (optional), UA, post-void residual, IPSS score.
cells.Treatment (Specific Drug/Dose): Tamsulosin 0.4 mg PO daily; Finasteride 5 mg PO daily for large prostates; Refractory → TURP.
cells.Patient Education: Avoid evening fluids/caffeine; meds take weeks to work; orthostatic precautions.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Often asymptomatic; obstructive symptoms late; bone pain in metastasis.
cells.Treatment (Specific Drug/Dose): Based on risk: surgery, radiation, androgen deprivation (Leuprolide 7.5 mg IM monthly).
cells.Patient Education: Discuss screening; treatment may cause sexual/urinary side effects.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Fever, perineal pain, urinary retention, boggy tender prostate.
cells.Diagnostics: UA + culture; do not massage prostate.
cells.Treatment (Specific Drug/Dose): Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID × 4–6 weeks or TMP-SMX DS BID × 4–6 weeks.
cells.Patient Education: Complete full therapy; warm baths; avoid irritants (caffeine, alcohol).

cells.Definition: Chronic pelvic pain w/ recurrent infections.
cells.Clinical Presentation: Recurrent UTIs, pelvic discomfort.
cells.Treatment (Specific Drug/Dose): Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID × 4–6 weeks or add alpha-blocker.
cells.Patient Education: May take months to improve; stress/pelvic floor therapy helpful.

cells.Definition: Infection of urinary tract (E. coli most common).
cells.Clinical Presentation: Dysuria, frequency, urgency; fever if complicated.
cells.Treatment (Specific Drug/Dose): Nitrofurantoin 100 mg BID × 7 days (if uncomplicated) TMP-SMX DS BID × 7–14 days Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BID × 7 days (complicated).
cells.Patient Education: Hydration; avoid bladder irritants; finish antibiotics; return if fever or flank pain.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Often asymptomatic; dysuria, discharge, pelvic pain.
cells.Patient Education: Treat partners; abstain 7 days; retest in 3 months.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Purulent discharge; dysuria; pelvic pain.
cells.Treatment (Drug + Dose): Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once (+ doxycycline if chlamydia not excluded).
cells.Patient Education: Treat partners; no sex for 7 days; retest if symptoms persist.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Green frothy discharge, strawberry cervix, itching.
cells.Patient Education: No alcohol with metronidazole; treat partners; abstain 7 days.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Painless chancre (primary), rash on palms/soles (secondary).
cells.Treatment (Drug + Dose): Penicillin G benzathine 2.4 million units IM once.
cells.Patient Education: Follow-up RPR titers; treat partners; avoid sex until cleared.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Painful grouped vesicles, ulcers, recurrent outbreaks.
cells.Treatment (Drug + Dose): Acyclovir 400 mg PO TID × 7–10 days (first episode).
cells.Patient Education: Avoid sex during outbreaks; condoms reduce but don’t eliminate risk.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Soft, flesh-colored papules.
cells.Treatment (Drug + Dose): Imiquimod 5% cream TIW × up to 16 weeks OR cryotherapy.
cells.Patient Education: HPV vaccine; recurrence common; safe sex practices.

cells.Clinical Presentation: Acute flu-like illness; chronic weight loss, infections.
cells.Treatment (Drug + Dose): ART started immediately (Biktarvy or equivalent first line).
cells.Patient Education: Lifelong therapy; prevent transmission; PrEP for partners.

cells.Definition: Degenerative joint disease characterized by progressive loss of articular cartilage, osteophyte formation, subchondral bone thickening
cells.Risk Factors: Age >45, obesity, joint injury, repetitive microtrauma, muscle weakness, genetics
cells.Clinical Presentation: Gradual onset joint pain worsened by activity, morning stiffness <30 min, crepitus, decreased ROM, often asymmetrical
cells.Diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis; X-ray may show joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis
cells.Pharmacologic Management: NSAIDs (oral or topical), acetaminophen, intra-articular corticosteroids
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Physical therapy, weight management, assistive devices, exercise (aerobic, strengthening)
cells.Patient Education: Chronic progressive disease, lifestyle modification, regular exercise, proper footwear, fall prevention

cells.Definition: Autoimmune, chronic inflammatory disorder primarily affecting synovial joints
cells.Risk Factors: Female sex, age 40–60, positive family history, genetics
cells.Clinical Presentation: Symmetric polyarthritis, morning stiffness >1 hr, tender/swollen joints (MCP, PIP, wrists), fatigue, systemic symptoms (low-grade fever)
cells.Diagnosis: Clinical + lab: RF, ACPA, ESR/CRP; imaging: MRI early, X-ray shows erosions
cells.Pharmacologic Management: NSAIDs, low-dose corticosteroids, DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine), biologics (TNF-alpha inhibitors)
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Rest, splints, PT/OT, adaptive devices, gentle exercise
cells.Patient Education: Disease education, self-management, medication adherence, monitor for flares, supportive resources

cells.Definition: Metabolic disorder with monosodium urate crystal deposition causing inflammatory arthritis
cells.Risk Factors: Male sex, obesity, high purine diet, alcohol, renal insufficiency, medications (diuretics, cyclosporine)
cells.Clinical Presentation: Acute monoarticular joint pain (first MTP “podagra”), redness, swelling, warmth, pain at rest and with weight-bearing, chronic tophi in untreated cases
cells.Diagnosis: Synovial fluid crystal analysis (definitive), uric acid levels, imaging may show erosions
cells.Pharmacologic Management: NSAIDs (indomethacin), corticosteroids, colchicine (acute), allopurinol/probenecid/uricase (chronic)
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Rest, ice, hydration, dietary modification
cells.Patient Education: Lifestyle changes, purine avoidance, weight management, alcohol moderation, trigger avoidance

cells.Definition: Loss of bone mineral density leading to increased fracture risk
cells.Risk Factors: Female post-menopause, low body weight, smoking, alcohol, vitamin D/calcium deficiency, chronic corticosteroid use, age
cells.Clinical Presentation: Often asymptomatic until fracture; may present with vertebral compression fracture, height loss, stooped posture, back pain
cells.Diagnosis: DEXA scan (T-score ≤ -2.5), FRAX calculator for fracture risk
cells.Pharmacologic Management: Calcium + vitamin D supplementation, bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate), hormone therapy if indicated
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Weight-bearing exercise, PT for balance/strength, fall prevention
cells.Patient Education: Long-term adherence to therapy, nutrition, exercise, fall prevention, smoking/alcohol moderation

cells.Definition: Inflammation of a bursa (fluid-filled sac) near joints
cells.Risk Factors: Repetitive motion, trauma, obesity, inflammatory disorders
cells.Clinical Presentation: Localized pain, swelling, tenderness over bursa, worsens with movement
cells.Pharmacologic Management: NSAIDs
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Rest, ice, compressive wraps, physical therapy, activity modification
cells.Patient Education: Avoid repetitive stress, use proper techniques, manage weight, self-monitor swelling

cells.Definition: Inflammation or degeneration of a tendon due to overuse
cells.Risk Factors: Repetitive activity, poor conditioning, age
cells.Clinical Presentation: Pain over tendon, swelling, warmth, pain with active motion
cells.Pharmacologic Management: NSAIDs, topical agents
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Rest, stretching, strengthening, activity modification, PT
cells.Patient Education: Gradual return to activity, ergonomic adjustments, adherence to rehab program

cells.Definition: Pain in cervical, thoracic, or lumbar spine; can be acute (<6 wks) or chronic (>12 wks)
cells.Risk Factors: Age, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, trauma, poor posture, heavy lifting
cells.Clinical Presentation: Localized or radiating pain, stiffness, limited ROM, radiculopathy (sciatica)
cells.Diagnosis: Clinical, imaging if red flags present (MRI, X-ray)
cells.Pharmacologic Management: NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, short-term opioids (rare)
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: PT, core strengthening, ergonomic modifications, heat/ice
cells.Patient Education: Posture, lifting techniques, exercise adherence, red-flag symptoms awareness

cells.Definition: Pain around knee joint, often from OA, meniscus injury, bursitis, patellofemoral pain
cells.Risk Factors: Age, obesity, previous injury, repetitive stress, overuse
cells.Clinical Presentation: Pain with weight-bearing, swelling, instability, locking/catching, morning stiffness
cells.Diagnosis: Clinical, X-ray for OA, MRI for meniscus/ligament
cells.Pharmacologic Management: NSAIDs, topical agents, intra-articular corticosteroids
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: PT, braces, activity modification, strengthening
cells.Patient Education: Weight management, exercise adherence, safe sports techniques

cells.Definition: Pain in glenohumeral or surrounding structures; rotator cuff or bursitis common
cells.Risk Factors: Overuse, trauma, age, poor posture
cells.Clinical Presentation: Pain with overhead activity, limited ROM, night pain, weakness
cells.Diagnosis: Clinical, X-ray, MRI if structural injury suspected
cells.Pharmacologic Management: NSAIDs, corticosteroid injection
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: PT, stretching, strengthening, activity modification
cells.Patient Education: Ergonomics, posture, activity pacing, proper exercise technique

cells.Definition: Pain from sprains, fractures, tendinitis, plantar fasciitis, neuromas
cells.Risk Factors: Trauma, repetitive stress, poor footwear, obesity, overuse
cells.Clinical Presentation: Swelling, redness, tenderness, limited ROM, plantar heel pain (fasciitis), burning/paresthesia (Morton’s neuroma)
cells.Diagnosis: Clinical, Ottawa ankle rules for fractures, X-ray/MRI if persistent
cells.Pharmacologic Management: NSAIDs, corticosteroid injections
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: RICE, bracing, PT, stretching (heel cord/plantar fascia), shoe modifications
cells.Patient Education: Footwear with arch support and wide toe box, gradual activity return, adherence to rehab

cells.Risk Factors: Age >65, osteoporosis, fall, low BMD, female sex
cells.Clinical Presentation: Pain in groin/hip, inability to bear weight, external rotation of leg, swelling
cells.Pharmacologic Management: Pain management (acetaminophen, opioids short-term)
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Surgical repair (ORIF, hip replacement), PT post-op
cells.Patient Education: Fall prevention, weight management, adherence to rehab, home safety

cells.Risk Factors: Osteoporosis, trauma, malignancy
cells.Clinical Presentation: Acute back pain, loss of height, kyphosis
cells.Pharmacologic Management: NSAIDs, short-term opioids, bisphosphonates for underlying osteoporosis
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Bracing, PT for posture/strength
cells.Patient Education: Fall prevention, bone health, medication adherence

cells.Risk Factors: Fall on outstretched hand, osteoporosis
cells.Clinical Presentation: Pain, swelling, dorsal wrist deformity (“dinner fork”)
cells.Pharmacologic Management: NSAIDs, acetaminophen
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Immobilization (cast/splint), PT after healing
cells.Patient Education: Fall prevention, safe techniques, bone health education

cells.Risk Factors: Overuse, sudden training increase, osteoporosis
cells.Clinical Presentation: Localized pain worsening with activity, relieved by rest
cells.Pharmacologic Management: NSAIDs if needed
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Activity modification, gradual return, PT
cells.Patient Education: Gradual training progression, proper footwear, bone health

cells.Risk Factors: Age <10, trauma
cells.Clinical Presentation: Pain, swelling, limited ROM, visible bend
cells.Pharmacologic Management: Pain control (acetaminophen/NSAIDs)
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Immobilization (cast/splint)
cells.Patient Education: Safe play, adherence to cast care, follow-up X-ray

cells.Definition / Overview: Anemia caused by insufficient iron for hemoglobin synthesis
cells.Diagnosis:
CBC (low Hgb/Hct),
Low Hgb (less than 12 or 13) 
 low MCV (less than 80; microcytic), 
low RBC
low ferritin < 30
high TIBCl > 400
TSAT < 20% 
Serum iron < 60

ANY of these findings should raise suspicion for iron deficiency
cells.Clinical Presentation:
Fatigue, pallor, dizziness, pica, koilonychia, exertional dyspnea, bleeding, melena, tachycardia, GI distress, 

Typically an incidental finding!!
cells.Pharmacologic Management:
First-line: Oral ferrous sulfate/gluconate/fumarate (manage GI se)- 3-6 months AFTER Hgb is met

Alternatives: IV iron (if malabsorption or intolerance), Blood transfusion if severe

Key tx indicatiors = anemia resolves upon iron admin, target ferritin = at least 50
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Dietary modification: iron-rich foods (red meat, legumes, spinach), vitamin C to enhance absorption
cells.Patient Education:
Take iron on empty stomach if tolerated, avoid antacids/tea with dose, expect dark stools, adherence critical for 3–6 months

Long-term management - oral iron every 3 months, IV iron check after each course
cells.Other Considerations:
NUMBER 1 DIFF is regular iron deficiency 

Iron def w/o anemia = normal Hgb synthesis, clinical manifestations of anemia 

Iron def w mild anemia = normocytic with a normal ARC, low ferritin/ Fe, increased transferring, increased unsat iron

cells.Definition / Overview: Anemia due to inadequate B12 causing impaired DNA synthesis
cells.Diagnosis:
CBC (macrocytic anemia)
high MCV >100
low serum B12
elevated homocysteine/methylmalonic acid
cells.Clinical Presentation: Fatigue, pallor, glossitis, neuropathy (paresthesia), gait disturbances
cells.Pharmacologic Management: First-line: Vitamin B12 supplementation (oral or IM injections); Alternatives: Cyanocobalamin nasal spray
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Dietary counseling for B12-rich foods (meat, dairy, fortified cereals)
cells.Patient Education: Lifelong supplementation may be needed if due to malabsorption; monitor neurologic symptoms

cells.Definition / Overview: Anemia due to insufficient folate affecting DNA synthesis
cells.Diagnosis: CBC (macrocytic anemia), low serum folate, normal B12
cells.Clinical Presentation: Fatigue, pallor, glossitis, mild neurologic symptoms absent
cells.Pharmacologic Management: First-line: Oral folic acid supplementation; Alternatives: Dietary folate intake
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Eat folate-rich foods (leafy greens, legumes, fortified grains)
cells.Patient Education: Take daily until deficiency corrected, important in pregnancy for neural tube defect prevention
cells.Other Considerations: Folate deficiency is rare in developed countries due to food fortification

cells.Condition:

MICROcytic Anemia
cells.Definition / Overview: Anemia associated with chronic inflammation, infection, or malignancy
cells.Diagnosis: CBC (normocytic or microcytic), low serum iron, low TIBC, normal/high ferritin
cells.Clinical Presentation: Fatigue, pallor; usually mild
cells.Pharmacologic Management: Treat underlying disease; Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) if severe; transfusions if needed
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Manage chronic condition; optimize nutrition
cells.Patient Education: Educate about underlying illness, monitor Hgb and iron studies, ESAs may require monitoring for hypertension or thromboembolism

cells.Definition / Overview: Bone marrow failure causing pancytopenia
cells.Clinical Presentation: Fatigue, pallor, bleeding/bruising, infections
cells.Pharmacologic Management: First-line: Immunosuppressive therapy (ATG + Cyclosporine); Alternatives: Hematopoietic stem cell transplant if eligible; transfusions
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Supportive care: infection prevention, bleeding precautions
cells.Patient Education: Lifelong follow-up; educate on infection risk, avoid medications/agents that suppress marrow

cells.Definition / Overview: Premature destruction of RBCs
cells.Diagnosis: CBC (anemia, reticulocytosis), elevated LDH, bilirubin, low haptoglobin, Coombs test if autoimmune
cells.Clinical Presentation: Fatigue, jaundice, dark urine, splenomegaly
cells.Pharmacologic Management: First-line: Corticosteroids for autoimmune; Alternatives: Immunosuppressants, Rituximab, Splenectomy, transfusions
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Avoid triggers (for G6PD deficiency: fava beans, certain drugs)
cells.Patient Education: Educate about signs of hemolysis, infection precautions, adherence to medications

cells.Definition / Overview: Genetic hemoglobinopathy causing RBC sickling
cells.Clinical Presentation: Pain crises, fatigue, pallor, jaundice, splenomegaly, vaso-occlusive complications
cells.Pharmacologic Management: First-line: Hydroxyurea; Alternatives: L-glutamine, chronic transfusions, bone marrow transplant
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Pain management, hydration, infection prevention
cells.Patient Education: Vaccinations critical, recognize pain crises early, avoid triggers (cold, dehydration)

cells.Definition / Overview: Genetic disorder causing decreased globin chain synthesis
cells.Diagnosis:
Low Hgb (less than 12 or 13) 
 low MCV (less than 80; microcytic), 
CBC (microcytosis), hemoglobin electrophoresis, genetic testing
cells.Clinical Presentation: Fatigue, pallor, skeletal changes in severe cases
cells.Pharmacologic Management: First-line: Regular transfusions for severe disease; Alternatives: Iron chelation therapy, Hydroxyurea, stem cell transplant
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Monitor growth/development, avoid iron overload
cells.Patient Education: Educate about transfusion schedules, iron overload management, routine follow-up

cells.Definition / Overview: Anemia secondary to reduced erythropoietin production
cells.Diagnosis: CBC (normocytic anemia), low EPO, elevated creatinine/BUN
cells.Clinical Presentation: Fatigue, pallor, dyspnea
cells.Pharmacologic Management: First-line: Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) with iron supplementation; Alternatives: transfusions if severe
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Optimize CKD management, dialysis support
cells.Patient Education: Monitor Hgb, iron studies, blood pressure; educate about ESA therapy and potential side effects

cells.Definition / Overview: Refer to hematologist or hospitalization IMMEDIATELY
cells.Diagnosis:
Hgb < 8 g/dL or Hct < 30% + symptomatic 
Chronic pts with acute exacerbations
cells.Clinical Presentation: Dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, dizziness
cells.Pharmacologic Management: Hospital

cells.Diagnosis:
Hgb <6-7 g/dL or Hct <30%; hemodynamic instability 
Acute hemorrhage (ICU)
cells.Clinical Presentation:
Hypotension, pallor, cold/clammy skin, abdominal bruising, thready pulse, tachycardia, dyspnea, altered mental status 
Risk for organ failure (ICU)
cells.Pharmacologic Management:
Immediate referral to ED 

Blood transfusion + fluid resuscitation + potential for procedure or intervention 
Referral to hematology once stable

cells.Definition / Overview: Bacterial infection caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, transmitted by Ixodes scapularis (deer tick)
cells.Diagnosis: Clinical (erythema migrans, exposure history), Two-step serology (ELISA → Western blot)
cells.Clinical Presentation: Early localized: erythema migrans (“bull’s-eye”), fever, malaise. Disseminated: multiple rashes, neurologic (Bell’s palsy, meningitis), cardiac (conduction abnormalities), musculoskeletal (arthritis)
cells.Pharmacologic Management: First-line: Doxycycline; Alternatives: Amoxicillin (children, pregnancy), Cefuroxime
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Tick avoidance (protective clothing, repellents), prompt tick removal
cells.Patient Education: Check for ticks after outdoor exposure, remove ticks promptly, monitor for rash/fever, complete antibiotic course

cells.Definition / Overview: Bacterial rickettsial infection caused by Rickettsia rickettsii, transmitted by Dermacentor and other ticks
cells.Diagnosis: Clinical (fever, rash, exposure history), Serology (IgM/IgG), PCR or biopsy if needed
cells.Clinical Presentation: Early: fever, headache, myalgia, maculopapular rash on wrists/ankles; Late: petechiae, CNS involvement, multiorgan failure
cells.Pharmacologic Management: First-line: Doxycycline (all ages); Alternatives: Chloramphenicol if doxycycline contraindicated
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Tick avoidance, prompt removal
cells.Patient Education: Seek medical care immediately if fever/rash develops after tick exposure, early treatment is critical

cells.Definition / Overview: Bacterial infection by Anaplasma phagocytophilum, transmitted by Ixodes ticks
cells.Diagnosis: PCR, serology, peripheral smear (morulae in granulocytes)
cells.Clinical Presentation: Fever, headache, malaise, myalgia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia
cells.Pharmacologic Management: First-line: Doxycycline; Alternatives: Rifampin in pregnancy
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Tick avoidance
cells.Patient Education: Monitor for high fever, seek early medical care, complete antibiotic course

cells.Definition / Overview: Bacterial infection by Ehrlichia chaffeensis, transmitted by Amblyomma (Lone Star) ticks
cells.Diagnosis: PCR, serology, peripheral smear (morulae in monocytes)
cells.Clinical Presentation: Fever, headache, malaise, myalgia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia
cells.Pharmacologic Management: First-line: Doxycycline; Alternatives: Rifampin in pregnancy
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Tick avoidance
cells.Patient Education: Early recognition critical, follow medication instructions carefully

cells.Definition / Overview: Parasitic infection by Babesia microti, transmitted by Ixodes ticks
cells.Clinical Presentation: Fatigue, fever, hemolytic anemia, jaundice, dark urine; may be severe in immunocompromised
cells.Pharmacologic Management: First-line: Atovaquone + Azithromycin (mild-moderate), Clindamycin + Quinine (severe)
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Tick avoidance
cells.Patient Education: Seek care if fever or hemolytic symptoms, prevent tick bites

cells.Definition / Overview: Bacterial infection caused by Francisella tularensis, transmitted via tick bite, animal contact
cells.Clinical Presentation: Ulceroglandular: ulcer at bite site, regional lymphadenopathy; other forms: pneumonic, oculoglandular
cells.Pharmacologic Management: First-line: Streptomycin or Gentamicin; Alternatives: Doxycycline, Ciprofloxacin
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Avoid tick bites, avoid handling wild animals without protection
cells.Patient Education: Use gloves when handling animals, report exposure to healthcare provider, complete antibiotic course

cells.Definition / Overview: Mild spotted fever rickettsial infection, transmitted by Gulf Coast tick
cells.Diagnosis: Clinical (eschar, fever, rash), PCR or serology
cells.Clinical Presentation: Fever, headache, myalgia, inoculation eschar, sparse maculopapular or papulovesicular rash
cells.Pharmacologic Management: First-line: Doxycycline; Alternatives: Chloramphenicol if doxycycline contraindicated
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Tick avoidance
cells.Patient Education: Early medical attention if fever or eschar develops, complete antibiotics

cells.Definition / Overview: Viral infection transmitted by Amblyomma ticks
cells.Clinical Presentation: Fever, fatigue, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia
cells.Pharmacologic Management: Supportive care only (no antiviral therapy)
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Tick avoidance
cells.Patient Education: Prevent tick bites, monitor symptoms, seek care if fever develops

cells.Definition / Overview: Viral infection transmitted by ticks
cells.Clinical Presentation: Fever, fatigue, myalgia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia
cells.Pharmacologic Management: Supportive care
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Tick avoidance
cells.Patient Education: Avoid tick exposure, early medical evaluation for febrile illness

cells.Definition / Overview: Viral infection by coltivirus, transmitted by Dermacentor ticks
cells.Clinical Presentation: Fever, headache, myalgia, photophobia, sometimes rash
cells.Pharmacologic Management: Supportive care
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Tick avoidance
cells.Patient Education: Check for ticks, remove promptly, symptomatic care

cells.Definition / Overview: Viral infection transmitted by Ixodes ticks
cells.Clinical Presentation: Fever, headache, vomiting, seizures, encephalitis; may cause long-term neurologic deficits
cells.Pharmacologic Management: Supportive care
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Tick avoidance
cells.Patient Education: Avoid tick habitats, early evaluation for neurologic symptoms

cells.Definition / Overview: Acute bacterial infection of dermis and subcutaneous tissue, usually from Strep pyogenes or S. aureus
cells.Diagnosis: Clinical; may culture wound if purulent; rule out abscess.
cells.Clinical Presentation: Erythema, warmth, tenderness, edema, poorly demarcated borders, may have fever.
cells.Pharmacologic Management: Mild: Cephalexin, Dicloxacillin; MRSA risk: TMP-SMX, Clindamycin, Doxycycline. Severe: IV Vancomycin.
cells.Non-Pharmacologic Management: Elevate affected limb, rest, warm compresses.
cells.Patient Education: Complete full antibiotic course; monitor for worsening/red streaking; prevent skin trauma.
